rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient that covers the full organic range at a moderate slope and temperature, maximizing the chance all 10 compounds elute and revealing the useful elution window. This first run will show whether retention is compressed, overly late, or missing so the next method can trim the window and adjust slope efficiently.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only score loss is from the last peak at 12.64 min; the next move is to shorten retention while preserving separation. The first run suggests all compounds elute within roughly phi_e 0.09–0.38, so a narrower, lower window plus higher temperature should keep everything in-gradient but pull the last peak closer to 10 minutes.

The compression in run 2 created a near-coelution at pair 6/7, so keep the same phi window and temperature but make the gradient shallower to restore spacing for the slope-sensitive region while likely keeping t_last near 10 minutes. This directly tests whether the bad pair is mainly a slope issue without reintroducing unnecessary retention from a broader window.

Runs 2 and 3 show pair 6/7 remains the limiting pair and does not recover enough with a shallower gradient, pointing to a selectivity problem rather than pure slope. Move to a broader, steeper window at the same higher temperature to change the phi region experienced by that pair while keeping the run fast enough to target t_last near or below 10 minutes.

The current best run is fast enough, so the only remaining gain is to improve the stubborn 6/7 selectivity; changing temperature is the most direct lever because that pair has responded inconsistently to slope. Keep the proven fast full-range gradient and drop to 25 C to test for a favorable selectivity shift while still likely staying under the 10-minute last-peak target.

Lowering temperature made selectivity much worse across the crowded middle, so test the opposite extreme while keeping the best gradient shape fixed. If the troublesome pair is temperature-sensitive, 60 C could improve 6/7 beyond the 50 C result without sacrificing the already ideal run time.

Temperature excursions away from 50 C hurt selectivity, so return to 50 C and now tune slope around the best run. A modest increase from 12 to 16 min should improve the limiting middle pair without the severe time penalty seen at 20 min, and t_last should still remain comfortably under 10 minutes.

The best results stay at 50 C with a fast gradient, but the limiting pair is still unresolved, so now adjust selectivity by trimming the high-organic end while keeping the low end fixed. Since all peaks in the scout eluted by about phi_e 0.38, reducing phi1 from 0.95 to 0.80 should alter the middle-window spacing without risking loss of the last compound or exceeding 10 minutes.

Trimming phi1 from 0.95 to 0.80 improved the limiting 6/7 pair while keeping all peaks under 10 minutes, so continue in the same direction with a slightly lower phi1. This probes whether the troublesome pair benefits from a tighter upper window before any hold-elution penalty appears.

The upper-window trim helped at 0.80 but got worse again at 0.75, suggesting the optimum may lie between 0.80 and 0.95 rather than lower. Try phi1 0.85 at the proven 12 min and 50 C to bracket the selectivity maximum for the persistent 6/7 pair while keeping a zero time penalty.

The best resolution for the stubborn pair among the phi1 trims is trending back upward as phi1 increases from 0.75 to 0.85, with the original 0.95 still best overall. Test the remaining bracket point at phi1 0.90 to check whether the local optimum sits just below 0.95 while retaining the zero time penalty.

The full-range window at 50 C remains best, and modestly lengthening the gradient worsened the critical pair, so test a slightly steeper slope than the current optimum. This checks whether the limiting 6/7 pair gains selectivity from additional compression while the last peak should still stay under 10 minutes.

Resolution of the limiting 6/7 pair improved when the gradient was made steeper from 12 to 10 min, while all peaks remained comfortably before 10 minutes. Test 8 min to see whether that trend continues and pushes the critical pair closer to full credit without any time penalty.

The best slope is now around 8–10 min, with 10 min slightly preferred because 8 min started to hurt another adjacent pair. Since 25 C and 60 C both worsened selectivity, probe a smaller temperature shift from the current optimum at 50 C; 45 C may improve the stubborn 6/7 selectivity without disrupting the rest of the chromatogram.

The best region is a steep full-range gradient near 50 C, and the disastrous 45 C result shows the critical pair is highly temperature-sensitive. Try the neighboring higher temperature with the stronger 8 min slope, aiming to improve the 6/7 pair beyond the current 0.97 while watching whether other middle pairs stay above 1.5.

At 55 C the 6/7 pair improved markedly but a new 4/5 coelution appeared only at the steeper 8 min slope, so back off slightly on slope while keeping the favorable higher temperature. This should test whether 10 min at 55 C balances both critical pairs better than either 10 min at 50 C or 8 min at 55 C.

Run 16 is the best so far, with only pair 4/5 still below full credit, so the logical next step is a slightly shallower gradient at the same favorable temperature. This should specifically test whether 4/5 continues to open enough to reach or approach R 1.5 while t_last remains safely below 10 minutes.

You already have a perfect score, so the only sensible different run is a nearby robustness check around the optimum. A slightly longer gradient at the same temperature should keep all pairs resolved and t_last under 10 minutes while confirming the plateau around the best conditions.

A different robustness probe is to test the lower-temperature side well away from the 55 C optimum while keeping the winning gradient shape fixed. This maps how sharply selectivity degrades versus temperature and helps confirm that the perfect method is not sitting on a narrow accidental optimum.

The optimum is already established, so use a remaining run to map the upper slope boundary at the best temperature. Extending to 16 min at 55 C will show how much resolution margin remains before the critical 6/7 pair falls below full credit, helping define the robustness window around the perfect method.

You already have the optimum, so continue defining the robustness boundary in gradient time at the best temperature. Since 16 min still scores very highly but loses full credit on 6/7, 18 min will help map how rapidly the critical pair degrades as the gradient becomes shallower.

With the optimum already found, use a remaining run to test whether the perfect result depends on the full upper organic range or whether a slightly narrower window is equally robust. Dropping phi1 to 0.90 at the winning tG and T should reveal whether the critical middle-region selectivity is sensitive to the upper endpoint.

You now have two perfect methods, so the next useful robustness check is to continue trimming the upper endpoint and find where the full-resolution plateau ends. Testing phi1 0.85 at the same optimal tG and T will show whether the method remains maximally scoring with a still narrower gradient window.

The optimum and its local robustness in phi1 and tG are already mapped, so use a remaining run to define the lower-temperature failure boundary more completely. Testing 30 C with the winning gradient shape will show how quickly the excellent 55 C selectivity collapses on cooling and strengthen confidence in the chosen operating region.

For the final run, test whether the perfect region can be made slightly faster while preserving full resolution by combining the successful 55 C temperature with the narrower upper window that also gave CRF 1.000. This probes whether 10 min is sufficient at phi1 0.90 to keep both critical pairs at or above 1.5 while shortening the method further.
